We gave several writers one opening sentence and asked for the rest of a creation myth, then set the results side by side without names. The opening reads: "In the world of the Tin Meadows, where the wind has a postal address, strange tales are told of the first word ever spoken."

A. They say that before the first word, the meadows rang only with the clatter of tin grass and the wind went undelivered, drifting from field to field with no place to call home. The Silversmith Mother, who had hammered the hills from a single kettle, grew lonely in all that ringing. So she cupped her hands, breathed into them, and folded the breath like a letter. Inside, she placed one word, though none agree on what it was. Some insist it was *here*, some swear it was *again*, and the oldest grandmothers say it was a name too round to say twice.

She sealed the breath with rust and gave it to the wind, writing upon it: *Number Seven, The Hollow Beneath the Weathervane*. The wind, delighted to finally have somewhere to be, carried it home. When the letter opened, the word spilled out and became the first bird, which has been trying to repeat it ever since.

B. The father of the Tin Meadows had a son, and his wife, the mother of the Tin Meadows, had a daughter. When the mother of the Tin Meadows gave birth to the daughter, the father of the Tin Meadows named her Heartbeat because the sound of her heart was heard before she was born.
The father of the Tin Meadows was a powerful man, and he had a horse that was very fast. One day, the father of the Tin Meadows decided to go on a journey, and he took his horse with him. The mother of the Tin Meadows said goodbye to her husband and watched as he rode off into the distance.
The father of the Tin Meadows rode for many days, and he came to a land where the grass was always green and the sky was always blue. He met a wizard there, and the wizard told him that he could grant him any wish. The father of the Tin Meadows wished for a son, and the wizard granted his wish.
The father of the Tin Meadows rode back to the Tin Meadows with his new son, and the mother of the Tin Meadows was overjoyed to see him.

C. It was not a prayer, nor a boast, but a simple exclamation of surprise: 'Ow!' The creature, with its yellow eyes and green, blue, and red stripes, possessed an uncanny ability to change its shape and color, much like a chameleon. Its voice was deep and booming, and it was said to be the most powerful creature in the universe, capable of speaking a language understood by all. This creature, known as the 'Ow!' creature, was a legend in the Tin Meadows, and its story continues to be passed down from generation to generation.
